title: Why Chinese Parents Don’t Want Two Kids
gist: China's pro-natalist loosening (two-child in 2015, three-child in 2021) produced no uptick in births; beyond child-rearing costs, James Palmer argues that the lived experience of pregnancy, childbirth and postpartum care—career penalties for women, hospital graft, high C-section rates, crowded multigenerational confinement—makes one child a 'one-and-done' choice for most couples.

insights.claim: China has experienced one of the sharpest fertility declines of any nation, especially since 2017, beyond the usual decline that accompanies rising wealth.
insights.speaker: James Palmer
insights.so_what: Accelerating demographic decline weighs on China's long-run growth, consumption and labor supply assumptions.
insights.quote: Fertility almost always declines as countries get richer, but China has seen one of the sharpest drops of any nation, especially since 2017.
insights.locator: The Realities of Having a Child in China

insights.claim: During much of the one-child policy era (1979-2015) the average Chinese couple had close to two children, but now that Beijing wants two, the average couple has only one.
insights.speaker: James Palmer
insights.so_what: Fertility outcomes are driven by social conditions rather than quotas, limiting Beijing's policy leverage over demographics.
insights.quote: Now that the government wants them to have two, the average couple has only one.
insights.locator: It’s a credit to public stubbornness

insights.claim: Loosening China's birth limits to two children in 2015 and three in 2021 produced no uptick in births, shocking officials.
insights.speaker: James Palmer
insights.so_what: Removing restrictions is insufficient; investors should discount pro-natalist policy announcements as birth-rate catalysts (e.g., for baby-goods demand).
insights.quote: It was a shock to officials that loosening the policy to two children in 2015 and then to three in 2021 produced no uptick in births.
insights.locator: It’s a credit to public stubbornness

insights.claim: China is the second-most expensive place in the world to raise a child, with the biggest costs arriving later as education expenses soar.
insights.speaker: James Palmer
insights.so_what: High education costs crowd out household consumption and suppress fertility simultaneously.
insights.quote: China is the second-most expensive place in the world to raise a child.
insights.locator: Commentary tends to focus on cost

insights.claim: China's 2021 ban on private K-12 tutoring did not cut child-raising costs; it created a gray market in which parents pay even more for tutors.
insights.speaker: James Palmer
insights.so_what: Demand for education services persisted after the crackdown, pushing spending into informal channels rather than eliminating it.
insights.quote: The government tried to solve this problem by banning private K-12 tutoring in 2021, but that only created a gray market where parents pay even more for tutors.
insights.locator: Commentary tends to focus on cost

insights.claim: The experience of pregnancy, childbirth and postpartum care, not just costs, is a major reason most Chinese parents stop after one child, according to the author's conversations with parents.
insights.speaker: James Palmer
insights.so_what: Suggests fertility policy focused only on financial subsidies will underdeliver unless maternity care and workplace norms change.
insights.quote: pregnancy, childbirth, and postpartum care are major reasons why having a kid is a one-and-done choice for most.
insights.locator: Yet in talking to Chinese parents

insights.claim: China has generous universal maternity leave on paper, but weak enforcement and widespread informal employment mean many women, especially those without a college degree, do not or cannot take it.
insights.speaker: James Palmer
insights.so_what: The gap between labor law and practice reflects a large informal workforce that blunts the reach of social policy.
insights.quote: because of weak enforcement and widespread informal employment, many women do not or cannot take it—particularly those without a college degree.

insights.claim: Despite gender discrimination being illegal in China, firms regularly advertise men-only roles or hire only married women who already have children, so even urban professional women risk being sidelined after childbirth.
insights.speaker: James Palmer
insights.so_what: Employer discrimination raises the opportunity cost of children for women, structurally depressing fertility and female labor productivity.
insights.quote: firms regularly advertise men-only roles or say that they will hire only married women who already have children.

insights.claim: Chinese government messaging that stresses child-raising as women's natural role has made the career-penalty problem worse rather than better.
insights.speaker: James Palmer
insights.so_what: Ideological framing of pro-natalism can be counterproductive, reducing the odds of a policy-driven fertility rebound.

themes.theme: Graft and C-sections in Chinese hospitals

insights.claim: Childbirth in Chinese public hospitals is nominally cheap and the government is pushing to make it free, but graft means parents usually pay bribes at every stage of the birthing process.
insights.speaker: James Palmer
insights.so_what: Headline 'free childbirth' subsidies may not reduce true out-of-pocket costs, limiting their fertility impact.
insights.quote: the medical system is rife with graft, and parents usually have to pay bribes at every stage of the birthing process.
insights.locator: This gap between policy and reality

insights.claim: China's overall cesarean section rate reached 44.5 percent in 2020, far above the 10 to 15 percent the World Health Organization considers normal.
insights.speaker: James Palmer
insights.so_what: Signals distorted incentives in China's hospital system, relevant to healthcare-sector economics and reform.
insights.quote: reaching an overall rate of 44.5 percent in 2020.

insights.claim: Chinese doctors push C-sections partly because they yield larger bribes and higher hospital billing, and the C-section rate drops significantly during anti-corruption campaigns.
insights.speaker: James Palmer
insights.so_what: Anti-corruption drives measurably change medical procedure volumes, a factor for hospital and medtech revenue in China.
insights.quote: during anti-corruption campaigns, the C-section rate drops significantly.

insights.claim: The birth experience in China is old-fashioned: parents have little say in medical decisions, fathers are rarely allowed in the delivery room, and postpartum depression follow-up is minimal.
insights.speaker: James Palmer
insights.so_what: Poor maternity care quality is an under-discussed deterrent to second births and a potential area for private healthcare demand.

insights.claim: Grandparents in China are widely expected to move in to help after a birth, which causes significant stress when young couples live far from hometowns in small apartments.
insights.speaker: James Palmer
insights.so_what: Urban migration and housing constraints interact with family norms to raise the non-financial cost of children.
insights.locator: That family presence is a primary source

insights.claim: Near-universal 'sitting the month,' a 30-to-40-day postpartum confinement in China, persists even though medical advice since the 1950s has tended against it due to risks like postpartum depression and deep vein thrombosis.
insights.speaker: James Palmer
insights.so_what: Cultural postpartum practices support a sizable paid-care market but add cost and strain to each birth.

insights.claim: The 1980s revival of postpartum confinement in China stemmed from the Mao era, when the practice was often banned and women were forced back into the fields soon after giving birth, leading that generation to pass stricter rules to their daughters.
insights.speaker: James Palmer
insights.so_what: Intergenerational cultural memory shapes consumer behavior around childbirth in ways policy struggles to change.

insights.claim: Young urban middle-class Chinese families are encouraged to hire an expensive live-in postpartum nurse for the confinement month, adding cost and crowding to already small homes.
insights.speaker: James Palmer
insights.so_what: Postpartum care services are a meaningful household expense category for China's urban middle class.
insights.quote: I know families where the new parents, both sets of grandparents, and a nurse were crammed into a small Beijing apartment.

insights.claim: Surrogacy is banned in China but increasingly common, with ongoing attempts to legalize it partly because surrogate-born babies can struggle to obtain a hukou residency document.
insights.speaker: James Palmer
insights.so_what: Possible future legalization of surrogacy would open a regulated fertility-services market in China.
insights.quote: Surrogacy is banned in China but increasingly common anyway.

insights.claim: China's surrogacy market ranges from gray to black, from organized illegal matching services to arrangements where surrogates may themselves be trafficked, and parents typically bribe hospitals for fake birth documents.
insights.speaker: James Palmer
insights.so_what: Shows strong latent demand for fertility services despite low birth rates, alongside governance and corruption risks.

insights.claim: Chinese couples will endure costly and stressful processes to have one child, but the data show they are very reluctant to repeat the experience.
insights.speaker: James Palmer
insights.so_what: Supports a base case of persistently sub-replacement fertility in China rather than a policy-driven rebound.
insights.quote: Chinese couples will endure all of this for the sake of a child. But the numbers show that they’re very reluctant to go through it twice.
insights.locator: On top of the surrogate’s fees
